name: The Bug-to-Test Writer
oneLiner: Turns a bug ticket — text plus screenshots — into a numbered, expected-result test case via a multimodal LLM, tracker-ready.
lead: Fetches a bug from ADO, loads a local briefing on its parent story, extracts up to four screenshots, and sends all of it to Gemini 2.0 Flash multimodal to draft a structured test: title, numbered steps, per-step expected results, and a repro-quality rating. Guarantees a sign-in first step, fills gaps from the story briefing, and falls back to a rule-based skeleton if no LLM key is set.
chore: Every fixed bug needs a clean test so a tester can confirm it and re-run it later. But reports are messy — one-line title, no steps, an unexplained screenshot. Turning that into a numbered test with a sensible expected result per step is skilled, tedious work, repeated per bug.
instead: A complete, ready-to-run test per bug — title, setup, numbered steps each with its own expected result, plus an honest good/partial/poor rating of the original report — serialized as Markdown, a tracker-upload Excel sheet, and optionally Word.
whyItMatters: A written test converts a one-time fix into a permanent regression net, and the reporter-quality leaderboard quietly surfaces who writes clear reports and who needs coaching.

howItWorks.step: Fetches the raw bug work item (`$expand=all`) and extracts the fields the test needs.
howItWorks.explain: The ingest step, hitting the ADO REST API directly rather than through a client wrapper. `$expand=all` is deliberate — it forces ADO to return the **full** field set including the HTML-bearing `System.Description` and `Microsoft.VSTS.TCM.ReproSteps`, which a default fetch omits and which the multimodal draft depends on. Auth is ADO's PAT convention: Basic auth with an **empty username** and the PAT as password (`:${pat}` base64-encoded), which is why the string starts with a bare colon. The `storyRef` regex mines the parent story straight out of the title — `US[_\s]?(\d{4,6})` tolerates `US1234`, `US_1234`, or `US 1234`, is case-insensitive, and captures only the digits so downstream code gets a clean number. Every field has a fallback (`priority` defaults to `3`, the rest to `''`) so a sparse ticket still yields a fully-typed `RawBug`.

howItWorks.step: Loads a local briefing on the bug's parent story to ground gap-filling — summary, acceptance criteria, business rules.
howItWorks.explain: The grounding step — it pulls **local** context about the parent story so the LLM can fill gaps in a thin bug without hallucinating product behavior. The story-number match has two fallbacks: try the title first, then `bug.storyRef`, and `storyNumMatch[1] || storyNumMatch[0]` copes with both patterns (the title regex has a capture group; the bare `\d{4,6}` on `storyRef` does not, so index 0 is the number). It probes each configured dir for `US-<num>.json`, `continue`-ing past misses and returning `empty` (with `found: false`) if none exist — a missing briefing is a normal, non-fatal case. The real point is the **trimming on the way out**: `summary` is capped at 600 chars, criteria to 10, rules to 8, and each array element is flattened to a string (`a.description || String(a)` tolerates both object and plain-string shapes). Only this bounded slice is ever handed to the model — the raw file never leaves disk, which both controls token cost and limits what's exposed.

howItWorks.step: Extracts up to four screenshots from the bug HTML — inline data URIs and ADO attachments — as base64.
howItWorks.explain: The multimodal input prep — it harvests images from both HTML fields (`descriptionHtml + reproStepsHtml`) so a screenshot pasted in either place is caught. The `while` loop condition ANDs the regex `exec` with `screenshots.length < MAX_IMAGES`, so the walk **stops early** once four images are collected rather than parsing the whole doc — a real cap on request size and token cost. It handles the two ways ADO embeds images differently: `data:image` URIs are already inline base64, split off after the comma, with a `base64.length > 100` guard that discards tracking pixels or truncated/garbage `src`s; `dev.azure.com` attachment URLs must instead be **fetched with the auth header** (they're access-controlled) and the `arrayBuffer` re-encoded to base64. Inline sources parse their real mime from the URI, while fetched attachments assume `image/png`. Each entry is tagged with its `source` so the prompt can label it.

howItWorks.step: Sends the prompt plus each screenshot to Gemini 2.0 Flash multimodal to draft the numbered test.
howItWorks.explain: The one network call to the model, built to Gemini's `generateContent` shape. The `parts` array interleaves modalities in a single content block: the combined system+user text first, then for each image an `inlineData` part (base64 + mime) **followed by** a text marker like `[Screenshot attached above — inline image]` — that trailing caption is what lets the model reason about *which* screenshot is which instead of seeing anonymous blobs. Two `generationConfig` choices are load-bearing: `temperature: 0.2` keeps the draft near-deterministic (test steps should be stable, not creative), and `maxOutputTokens: 8192` leaves room for a long numbered test with per-step expected results without truncation. The response is dug out defensively — `data.candidates?.[0]?.content?.parts?.[0]?.text || ''` returns `''` rather than throwing if Gemini blocks the response or returns no candidate, which is exactly the empty string the caller's parse-or-fallback path is written to handle.

howItWorks.step: Assembles the final test case, guaranteeing a sign-in first step and falling back to a skeleton if the LLM is unavailable.
howItWorks.explain: The orchestrator that ties context-gathering, the model call, and normalization together — and it's built so the agent **always** produces a usable test, never nothing. The LLM path is guarded twice: `GOOGLE_API_KEY` gates whether Gemini is even called (no key → straight to `buildFallbackTestCase`), and the second `if (!llmOutput)` catches the case where the key exists but `parseLLMJson` fails on malformed model output — both collapse to the same rule-based skeleton. Screenshots are only extracted when `input.includeScreenshots` is set (the `--no-screenshots` escape hatch). The post-processing is the invariant that makes every emitted test runnable: if the first step's `action` doesn't mention `navigate`, it `unshift`s a canonical sign-in step and then **renumbers the whole array** so `stepNumber` stays 1..N contiguous — a tester can't run step 3 without first being logged in. `qualityAssessment` defaults to `'poor'` so a rating is never absent.

howItWorks.step: Aggregates the good/partial/poor ratings per reporter into a scored, ranked leaderboard.
howItWorks.explain: The leaderboard builder — it turns the per-bug `qualityAssessment` ratings into a per-reporter quality score. The bucketing exploits the fact that `qualityAssessment` is exactly one of `good`/`partial`/`poor`, so `map.get(name)![tc.qualityAssessment]++` uses the rating string **as the object key** to increment the right counter in one line, with `reportedBy || 'Unknown'` catching unattributed tickets. The score is a weighted average where `partial` counts as **half** a good report (`counts.good + counts.partial * 0.5`) over `total`, scaled to a 0–100 percentage — so someone with all-`good` reports scores 100 and all-`poor` scores 0. The `total > 0` guard is defensive against an empty bucket. The final sort is descending by `score`, with `b.total - a.total` as the tiebreak so that among equal scores the higher-volume reporter ranks first — rewarding a sustained track record over a lucky one-off.

examples.caption: One-line bug, zero steps → real test
examples.input: Bug #204 `Summary button does nothing`, no repro steps, one screenshot.
examples.output: Test `Verify the Summary button produces a summary`: step 1 sign-in, steps to open a session and click Summary, each with an expected result — rated `poor` (no original steps). The screenshot fed the multimodal draft.

examples.caption: Well-written bug, faithful turnaround
examples.input: Bug #318 with clear numbered steps and an error-state screenshot.
examples.output: A step-by-step test mirroring the reporter's steps and confirming correct behavior, rated `good`, plus a tracker-upload `.xlsx` row.

examples.caption: Reporter-quality leaderboard
examples.input: `--bug-ids` with ten tickets from several reporters.
examples.output: Ten generated tests plus a ranked table of each reporter's good/partial/poor mix and weighted score — a data-backed nudge on report quality.

underHood.heading: Fetch the bug from ADO
underHood.output: Title, description, repro steps, priority, severity, reporter — via the REST API with `$expand=all`.

underHood.heading: Load local story briefing
underHood.input: The bug's linked user story number.
underHood.output: A trimmed local `US-<num>.json` — summary, flows, rules, acceptance criteria — for gap-filling, never sent wholesale to the model.

underHood.heading: Extract screenshots
underHood.input: Images embedded in or attached to the bug.
underHood.output: Up to four base64 images (inline or attachment), ready to attach to the request.

underHood.heading: Draft with the multimodal LLM
underHood.output: A structured test case — title, numbered steps with expected results, repro-quality rating — from Gemini 2.0 Flash (or the rule-based fallback).

underHood.heading: Serialize the batch
underHood.output: Markdown, a tracker-upload `.xlsx`, optionally `.docx` — plus the weighted reporter-quality leaderboard.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
An Azure DevOps org/project and a **PAT** with work-item read scope.
One or more bug IDs — already-filed tickets with at least a title and, ideally, a description or screenshots.
A **Google Gemini API key** — bug text and screenshots are sent to the multimodal model to draft the test; without a key it drops to a rule-based skeleton.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is TypeScript on Node. One-time per machine.
steps.firstRun: First time only, on a new machine.

steps.label: Clone and install dependencies.
steps.why: `npm install` pulls the ADO client, the Gemini client, and the `xlsx`/Word writers into `node_modules`.
steps.firstRun: Full install, a minute or two.
steps.rerun: No-op once installed, unless the dependency list changed.

steps.label: Export the ADO target and the Gemini key (environment variables).
steps.cmd:
export ADO_ORGANIZATION=my-org
export ADO_PROJECT="My Project"
export ADO_PAT=your-access-token
export GOOGLE_API_KEY=your-gemini-key
steps.why: Read at startup to resolve the board and the drafting model. Leave `GOOGLE_API_KEY` unset and it still runs on the rule-based fallback.

steps.label: Dry-run to fetch the bugs — no LLM call.
steps.why: `--dry-run` fetches and reads the bugs only — no Gemini call, no files — a quick check that the IDs and access resolve.

steps.label: Generate the real test cases.
steps.cmd:
npm run bug:tc -- --bug-ids "4397,4262,4488"
# skip sending screenshots to the AI:
npm run bug:tc -- --bug-ids "4397" --no-screenshots
# also produce a Word document:
npm run bug:tc:word -- --bug-ids "4397"
steps.why: The real run — one LLM-drafted test per bug ID, each starting with sign-in and ending with the fix confirmed.
steps.rerun: No caching — the same IDs re-fetch and re-draft from scratch, so an improved bug description flows through on the next run.

steps.label: Open the generated tests.
steps.why: The `.md` is the readable draft; the `.xlsx` is pre-shaped for bulk upload into the tracker as real test cases.

inputs.name: --bug-ids <ids>
inputs.desc: Comma-separated bug IDs to generate tests for (required).

inputs.name: --app-url <url>
inputs.desc: Environment URL the generated test's sign-in step points at.

inputs.name: --no-screenshots
inputs.desc: Skip extracting and sending screenshots — text-only draft.

inputs.name: --dry-run
inputs.desc: Fetch bugs only — skip the LLM generation step.

inputs.name: environment variables
inputs.desc: Org/project target, the PAT, and the Gemini key.

outputs.name: BugTC_<timestamp>.json
outputs.desc: Full structured test cases — title, steps, expected results, repro-quality rating per bug.

outputs.name: BugTC_<timestamp>.md
outputs.desc: The same tests rendered to read and follow.

outputs.name: BugTC_ADO_Upload_<timestamp>.xlsx
outputs.desc: Tracker-shaped sheet for bulk-uploading the tests as real test cases.

runbook.rerun: No caching — the same bug ID re-fetches the ticket and re-drafts from scratch, so an improved description or a newly-added screenshot flows through automatically on re-run.
runbook.integrate: Trigger it the moment a bug flips to Resolved (an ADO webhook or state-change hook) with that bug's ID, then hand the `.xlsx` to your bulk test-case importer — 'fixed' becomes 'has a permanent regression test' with no manual writing in between.

video.caption: A 2-3 minute screen recording: a messy bug report becomes a numbered, ready-to-run test via multimodal LLM.
script: Open a terminal beside the bug ticket in the browser so viewers can compare the two.
Say: 'This agent reads a bug report — even a messy one — and writes the test that proves it's really fixed. Watch.'
Show the bug ticket: a short title, thin description, one screenshot.
Run `node -v` and `npm install` (or note it's already done); one line each on what they do.
Show the `export ADO_ORGANIZATION / ADO_PROJECT / ADO_PAT / GOOGLE_API_KEY` lines; note the AI key is what lets it read the screenshot too.
Run the command with `--dry-run` first; point out it just confirms the bug was fetched.
Run it for real; narrate as it calls the AI model with the bug text and screenshot together.
Open the produced `.md`; read out step 1 (always sign-in), the numbered steps, and the expected result on each.
Point out the repro-quality rating it gave the original report — 'poor,' in this case — and explain why.
Close: 'That test now lives in the tracker forever — the next regression won't get past it.'
